title: Emergency Fund Basics
text: An emergency fund is a dedicated savings reserve covering 3 to 6 months of essential living expenses. It provides a financial buffer against unexpected events such as job loss, medical emergencies, or major repairs, preventing the need to liquidate long-term investments or take on high-interest debt. Liquid accounts such as savings accounts or money market funds are appropriate vehicles for emergency reserves.

title: Debt Avalanche Strategy
text: The debt avalanche method prioritizes repayment of debts with the highest interest rates first, while making minimum payments on all remaining obligations. This strategy minimizes the total interest paid over the life of all debts and is mathematically optimal for reducing debt cost, particularly for high-APR obligations such as credit cards with rates above 15-20% APR.

title: Retirement Readiness and Longevity Planning
text: Retirement readiness is assessed by comparing projected portfolio value at retirement with the income replacement target. A common benchmark is replacing 70-80% of pre-retirement gross income. The gap between projected wealth and required income is the retirement shortfall, which drives monthly contribution targets. Longevity risk — the risk of outliving assets — is a central concern in withdrawal sequencing strategies.

title: Portfolio Rebalancing and Drift Management
text: Portfolio rebalancing is the process of realigning asset class weights back to a target allocation after market movements cause drift. Regular rebalancing — either on a fixed schedule or when drift exceeds a threshold such as 5% — maintains the intended risk profile. Rebalancing enforces a disciplined buy-low, sell-high discipline by systematically trimming outperforming assets and adding to underperforming ones.

title: Goal Shortfall Resolution — Edelman Three-Option Solver
text: When a financial goal has a projected shortfall, three mathematical resolution paths exist. Option A increases monthly contributions to close the gap by the target date. Option B reduces the target amount to the maximum supportable by current savings and timeline. Option C extends the timeline until current contribution levels are sufficient. Each option represents a different trade-off between savings effort, lifestyle adjustment, and time horizon flexibility.
